0.title: Course Introduction
0.content:
When people mention Chenin Blanc, most immediately think of sweet Layon or Vouvray in many sweetness levels. But the stage where Chenin truly shows its "astonishing ageing potential" is actually the bone-dry Anjou Blanc and Saumur Blanc. These two AOCs are the entry-level classics of dry Chenin Blanc and the best starting point for judging Chenin.

Learning Objectives

🍇 Chenin Blanc varietal character

Grasp Chenin's acidity, phenolic compounds, aromatic range and ripeness differences

🪨 Anjou Noir vs Saumur Blanc

Tell apart the two completely different terroir logics of black schist and white tuffeau

🛢️ Winemaking choices

The influence of stainless-steel tanks vs large old oak casks vs amphorae

🌟 Role-model producers

Know representative producers such as Domaine des Roches Neuves, Domaine du Closel and Nicolas Joly
1.title: Chenin Blanc — The Complete Profile
1.componentProps.slide.title: Chenin Blanc — The Complete Profile
1.componentProps.slide.description: One of the world's most expressive white grapes — able to make dry, off-dry, botrytised sweet, sparkling and New World dry wines, with every origin point found in the Loire
2.title: Anjou Blanc and Saumur Blanc — Two Terroir Philosophies
2.highlights.0.content: Black Anjou — mainly Brioverian schist, dark soils, strong mineral tension
2.highlights.1.title: Saumur Blanc terroir
2.highlights.1.content: Dominated by tuffeau, the same as Vouvray — chalky minerality, elegant balance
2.highlights.2.title: Same variety, different personalities
2.highlights.2.content: Anjou Blanc is more exuberant, Saumur Blanc more restrained and elegant
2.content:
Although the Anjou Blanc and Saumur Blanc AOCs are geographically adjacent and share the same variety, Chenin Blanc, the dramatic difference in soils — black schist vs white tuffeau — gives them completely different personalities, which is why the middle Loire is called the "museum of Chenin terroir."

🌑 Anjou Blanc

  • Geography: Anjou Noir (Black Anjou), southwest Maine-et-Loire
  • Soils: Brioverian schist (late Precambrian, blue-black) + some volcanic rock
  • Area: about 1,000 hectares
  • Rules: ≥ 80% Chenin Blanc, ≤ 20% Sauvignon Blanc/Chardonnay may be blended
  • Sweetness: mostly dry (Sec), a few Demi-Sec
  • Style: exuberant, deep minerality, flint + graphite aromas, solid body
  • Ageing: top wines 5–10 years

⚪ Saumur Blanc

  • Geography: around the town of Saumur, where the Loire and Thouet rivers meet
  • Soils: mainly tuffeau (late Cretaceous), some limestone
  • Area: about 800 hectares
  • Rules: ≥ 80% Chenin Blanc, ≤ 20% Sauvignon Blanc/Chardonnay may be blended
  • Sweetness: mainly Sec
  • Style: chalky minerality, white flowers, green apple, lemon peel, elegant balance
  • Ageing: top wines 5–8 years

🔍 One-line distinction:

Anjou Blanc is Chenin's "trail runner" — strong, deeply mineral, a little wild.
Saumur Blanc is Chenin's "ballet dancer" — elegant, light, finely chalky.
2.quiz.question: What is the key terroir difference between Anjou Blanc and Saumur Blanc?
2.quiz.options.1: Soil — Anjou is mainly schist, Saumur mainly tuffeau
2.quiz.explanation: Both AOCs require ≥ 80% Chenin Blanc, with similar climate and rules. The key difference is the soil: Anjou Noir's Brioverian schist (Precambrian, blue-black) vs Saumur's tuffeau (Cretaceous, snow-white and porous). This geological boundary gives Chenin Blanc on the two sides entirely different mineral textures: the "graphite/flint" of schist vs the "chalk/wet stone" of tuffeau.

4.title: Savennières — The Pinnacle of Anjou Dry Whites
4.highlights.0.title: A top sub-region
4.highlights.0.content: Located within Anjou, producing only dry Chenin Blanc white wines
4.highlights.1.title: Volcanic-rock terroir
4.highlights.1.content: Rare in Anjou — a mix of volcanic rock and schist gives a distinctive tropical mineral tension
4.highlights.2.title: Two separate crus
4.highlights.2.content: Coulée de Serrant (7 hectares, sole ownership) and La Roche-aux-Moines
4.content:
Savennières is the top sub-AOC within Anjou Blanc, independent of the main AOC system and regarded as the world benchmark for dry Chenin Blanc. Its special geology — volcanic rock + schist + sand — lets Chenin show extremely concentrated mineral depth and ageing potential (top wines can be kept 30+ years).

📐 Savennières rules

  • Area: about 145 hectares
  • Variety: 100% Chenin Blanc
  • Sweetness: the vast majority is dry (Sec, residual sugar ≤ 4 g/L, up to 8 g/L when balanced by acidity); the rules also allow demi-sec/moelleux/doux in overripe vintages, but this is rare
  • Maximum yield: dry 50 hL/ha (sweet 35 hL/ha)
  • Harvest: must be by hand, multiple passes permitted

🌟 Two separate Cru AOCs

  • Coulée de Serrant: 7 hectares, solely owned by the Nicolas Joly family (Domaine de la Coulée de Serrant) (bought in 1962; the vineyard itself was cleared by monks from 1130). Joly is a global pioneer of biodynamics, and his wines are seen as one of the spiritual origins of the "natural wine" movement
  • La Roche-aux-Moines: 33 hectares, shared among several estates. Representative producers: Domaine aux Moines, Château de Chamboureau

🍷 Style characteristics

When young: green apple, quince, chamomile, white flowers, flint minerality → with tight acidity and a phénolique texture (Chenin's characteristic slight bitterness/grip, like grapefruit pith).

With age: beeswax, roasted hazelnut, Madeira-style oxidative notes, curry, hay — the 10–30 year ageing potential is the greatest among Loire dry whites.

6.title: The Influence of Winemaking on Dry Chenin
6.highlights.0.title: Stainless-steel tank
6.highlights.0.content: Preserves pure fruit and mineral tension; the mainstream for entry-level wines
6.highlights.1.title: Old oak cask
6.highlights.1.content: Favoured by top estates — it doesn't bring obvious oak flavour, but adds depth of texture
6.highlights.2.title: Amphora / concrete egg
6.highlights.2.content: A new trend — adds complexity while preserving mineral purity
6.content:
Chenin Blanc reacts to oak very differently from Chardonnay — it dislikes the "vanilla + cream" tone of new barrels and fits "neutral vessels" better. That is why Loire dry Chenin mostly uses large old oak casks (500–600 L Demi-Muid) rather than the standard 225 L barrique.

🥶 Stainless-steel tank (Cuve Inox)

  • Character: precise temperature control, no oxidation, no flavour added
  • Preserves: fresh fruit, minerality, pure acidity
  • Suited to: entry-level Anjou Blanc, Saumur Blanc, Vouvray Sec
  • Downside: lacks depth of texture, limited ageing potential

🛢️ Large old oak cask (Demi-Muid 500–600 L)

  • Character: large capacity, slow release of oak flavour, micro-oxidation
  • Effect: adds no obvious oak flavour, but makes the wine rounder and the structure firmer
  • Suited to: top Savennières, Saumur Premier Cru, top Vouvray Sec
  • Role models: Domaine du Closel, Château d'Epiré, Roches Neuves

🏺 Amphora / concrete egg (Amphora / Tinaja / Concrete Egg)

  • Character: no flavour added, allows tiny amounts of oxygen, natural convection
  • Effect: both pure minerality and a rounded texture
  • Suited to: new-generation natural winemaking
  • Role models: Vincent Carême, Domaine de la Sénéchalière

🌀 Lees ageing (Sur lie / Bâtonnage)

Many top dry Chenins stay in contact with the lees in the vessel for 6–18 months, with regular stirring (bâtonnage). This technique gives Chenin extra roundness of texture, nutty aromas and more stable resistance to oxidation, and is common practice in Saumur Blanc and Savennières.
6.quiz.question: Why is brand-new 225L oak used less often for dry Chenin Blanc?
6.quiz.options.0: Chenin is unsuited to any oak contact
6.quiz.options.1: Chenin's aromas are delicate, and the vanilla/cream tones of new barrels easily overpower varietal character; Loire winemakers prefer large old casks or neutral vessels
6.quiz.options.2: It is prohibited by the rules
6.quiz.explanation: Chenin Blanc's aromatic range (green apple, quince, white flowers, minerals) is very delicate, and the vanilla, cream and toast tones from new barrels easily mask varietal and terroir character. That is why the Loire's top Chenins (Savennières, Saumur Blanc, Vouvray Sec) mostly use 500–600L Demi-Muid casks or neutral stainless steel/concrete eggs. By contrast, Chardonnay (such as in Burgundy) integrates better with new-barrel aromas.
7.title: Level 3-1 Knowledge Check
7.questions.0.question: What is the minimum proportion of Chenin Blanc in Anjou Blanc AOC?
7.questions.0.explanation: Anjou Blanc requires ≥ 80% Chenin Blanc, with ≤ 20% Sauvignon Blanc and/or Chardonnay allowed. This flexibility lets estates adjust style — most top wines still choose 100% Chenin, and a few blend in Sauvignon to add aroma. The rules for Saumur Blanc are the same.
7.questions.1.question: What is Savennières' main sweetness style?
7.questions.1.options.0: Sec / Demi-Sec / Moelleux, all of them
7.questions.1.options.1: Mainly dry (Sec), with the rules also permitting a small amount of off-dry / sweet
7.questions.1.explanation: The vast majority of Savennières is dry (Sec: residual sugar ≤ 4 g/L, up to 8 g/L when balanced by acidity). The rules do not forbid sweet styles — demi-sec, moelleux or doux can still be made in overripe vintages (with lower maximum yields) — but the market is almost entirely dry whites, letting Chenin's terroir differences show directly.
7.questions.2.question: Which biodynamic pioneer solely owns Coulée de Serrant?
7.questions.2.explanation: Coulée de Serrant is a separate Cru AOC within Savennières, only 7 hectares, cleared by monks from 1130 and bought by the Joly family in 1962. From the 1980s Nicolas Joly converted it to biodynamic farming, becoming the spiritual leader of the global biodynamic wine movement. His book "Wine from Sky to Earth" is a classic in the field.
7.questions.3.question: Why do Loire dry Chenins prefer large Demi-Muid (500–600 L) oak casks?
7.questions.3.options.1: Large casks release oak flavour slowly, adding depth of texture without masking Chenin's delicate varietal character
7.questions.3.explanation: The ratio of wood surface area to wine volume in Demi-Muids (500L) and foudres (large wooden vats) is much smaller than in the standard barrique (225L), so oak flavour is released more slowly and gently. This matters especially for a delicately aromatic variety like Chenin Blanc — it gains the benefits of rounded texture and micro-oxidation without being masked by the vanilla/cream flavours of new barrels.
